hook: A surveyor cannot climb a 30-meter tree to measure it, and a builder cannot guess how steep a ramp is. Both stand back, measure one angle and one length, and let a ratio of sides do the rest. Those ratios, sine, cosine and tangent, are the starting point for every periodic function in this unit.

prereq.q: A line rises 6 units while it runs 8 units to the right. What is its slope?

figure.caption: The names of the two legs depend on which acute angle you stand at; the hypotenuse is always across from the right angle.

chain.cause: Stand at an acute angle $\theta$ of a right triangle
chain.effect: the leg across from $\theta$ is the opposite side, the leg touching $\theta$ is the adjacent side, and the side across from the right angle is the hypotenuse

chain.cause: Right triangles with the same angle $\theta$ are similar
chain.effect: the ratios of their sides are the same, whatever the triangle's size, so each ratio depends only on $\theta$

chain.cause: You know one side and the angle
chain.effect: pick the ratio that links the known side to the unknown one, write the equation, and solve it

ideas: The hypotenuse is the longest side, so $\sin\theta$ and $\cos\theta$ are between $0$ and $1$ for an acute angle.
$\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$ is rise over run: the slope of the hypotenuse when the adjacent side lies flat.
To find a side: write the ratio, put in the known values, then multiply (unknown on top) or divide (unknown on the bottom).

misconception.wrong: The opposite side is always the vertical side and the adjacent side is always the horizontal one.
misconception.right: Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you use. Switch to the other acute angle and the two legs swap names; only the hypotenuse stays the same.

summary: In a right triangle, name the legs from the angle $\theta$: opposite and adjacent. Then $\sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, $\cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$ and $\tan\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$. The ratios depend only on the angle, so one angle and one side are enough to find the other sides.
